title: Possible Strongyloides stercoralis infection diagnosed by videocapsule endoscopy in an immunocompetent patient with devastating diarrhea
case_text: A 70-year-old, housewife, living in a small village, presented with a six-month history of more than 10 watery diarrheas per day and loss of 18 kilos of body weight. Laboratory data were normal, including hemoglobin, white cell count and differential, CRP, serum albumin and immunoglobulin, iron, feritin, vitamin B12, and folate. Chest x-ray was normal. ESR was 40 mm/h. Stool examination for hemoglobin, leukocytes, parasites and cultures for pathogens was negative (twice). Colonoscopy with biopsies was normal. Duodenal biopsies showed mild, non-diagnostic changes of mucosa villi. Antibodies to tissue transglutaminase, endomysial antibodies and serum chromogranin-A were negative, including HIV infection. A small bowel videocapsule endoscopy (SBVCE) study showed mucosal areas of denuded villi and prominent small bowel submucosal vessels in the jejunum, multiple linear whitish lesions surrounded by reddish mucosa (Fig. 1), and parasites within the ileal fluid, entering the ileal mucosa (Fig. 2). These SBVCE findings favored the diagnosis of Strongyloides stercoralis infection. Review of previous histology of small bowel and colon, two more stool examinations for parasites and serum IgG antibodies against Strongyloides stercoralis (ELISA) were negative. She also tested negative for the HTLV-1 co-infection. The patient was treated with two cycles of albendazole 400 mg/d for 7 days. At 6-month follow up, she had no diarrhea and gained 4 kg of body weight.

   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Soil-Transmitted Helminths
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Strongyloides stercoralis infection diagnosed by videocapsule endoscopy
